steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the lead section of an encyclopedia article on abstract semantic graphs (term graphs) in computer science: what they are, how they differ from abstract syntax trees, and how they are used and built.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Definition: ASG / term graph
- Comparison with abstract syntax trees; shared subterms
- Terminology: term graph vs abstract semantic graph
- Why trees can't share, and why ASGs are used in compilers
- How an ASG is built from an AST

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Definition
  - ASG = term graph; a form of abstract syntax
  - expression of formal/programming language represented by graph; vertices = subterms
  - higher abstraction level than AST (which expresses syntactic structure of expression/program)
- Shared subterms
  - more complex and concise than ASTs: may contain shared subterms ("common subexpressions")
  - often compiler intermediate representation, storing results of common subexpression elimination on ASTs
  - ASTs are trees -> can't represent shared terms
  - usually DAGs; some applications allow cycles, e.g. recursive expressions in functional languages as non-looping iteration constructs
  - mutability of these graphs studied in graph rewriting
- Terminology
  - "term graph": term graph rewriting (transforming/processing expressions via rewriting rules)
  - "abstract semantic graph": linguistics, programming languages, type systems, compilation
- Trees vs sharing
  - node in proper tree can't have more than one parent
  - simple, but redundant representation, possibly duplicated computation of identical terms
  - so ASGs used as intermediate language at compilation stage after AST construction via parsing
- Construction
  - from AST by enrichment and abstraction
  - enrichment e.g. back-pointers: edges from identifier node (variable use) to declaration node
  - abstraction: remove details relevant only in parsing, not semantics

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In computer science an abstract semantic graph (ASG), also called a term graph, is a form of abstract syntax where an expression of a formal or programming language is represented by a graph, and the vertices of the graph are the subterms of the expression. An ASG is at a higher level of abstraction than an abstract syntax tree (or AST), which is used to express the syntactic structure of an expression or program.

ASGs are more complex and more concise than ASTs, because they can contain shared subterms (which are also called "common subexpressions"). Compilers often use abstract semantic graphs as an intermediate representation to store the results of doing common subexpression elimination on abstract syntax trees. ASTs are trees, so they can't represent shared terms. ASGs are usually directed acyclic graphs (DAG), but some applications may allow graphs that contain cycles. For example a graph with a cycle could be used to represent recursive expressions, which are commonly used in functional programming languages as iteration constructs that don't loop. The mutability of these kinds of graphs is studied in the field of graph rewriting.

- Terminology
  - "term graph": term graph rewriting (transforming/processing expressions via rewriting rules)
  - "abstract semantic graph": linguistics, programming languages, type systems, compilation
- Trees vs sharing
  - node in proper tree can't have more than one parent
  - simple, but redundant representation, maybe duplicated computation of identical terms
  - so ASGs used as intermediate language at stage after AST construction via parsing
- Construction
  - from AST by enrichment and abstraction
  - enrichment e.g. back-pointers from identifier node (variable use) to its declaration node
  - abstraction: remove details only relevant in parsing, not semantics

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In computer science an abstract semantic graph (ASG), also called a term graph, is a form of abstract syntax where an expression of a formal or programming language is represented by a graph, and the vertices of the graph are the subterms of the expression. An ASG is at a higher level of abstraction than an abstract syntax tree (or AST), which is used to express the syntactic structure of an expression or program.

ASGs are more complex and more concise than ASTs, because they can contain shared subterms (which are also called "common subexpressions"). Compilers often use abstract semantic graphs as an intermediate representation to store the results of doing common subexpression elimination on abstract syntax trees. ASTs are trees, so they can't represent shared terms. ASGs are usually directed acyclic graphs (DAG), but some applications may allow graphs that contain cycles. For example a graph with a cycle could be used to represent recursive expressions, which are commonly used in functional programming languages as iteration constructs that don't loop. The mutability of these kinds of graphs is studied in the field of graph rewriting.

The name term graph goes with the field of term graph rewriting, which is about transforming and processing expressions by specifying rewriting rules. The name abstract semantic graph is used when people talk about linguistics, programming languages, type systems and compilation.

Abstract syntax trees can't share subexpression nodes, because a node in a proper tree can't have more than one parent. This is simple conceptually, which is appealing, but it can cost a redundant representation and that can mean computing identical terms more than once, which is inefficient. Because of this ASGs are often used as an intermediate language at a compilation stage that comes after the abstract syntax tree has been built by parsing.

Usually an abstract semantic graph is built from an abstract syntax tree by a process of enrichment and abstraction. For example the enrichment can be adding back-pointers, which are edges from an identifier node (where a variable is used) to a node that represents the declaration of that variable. The abstraction can mean removing details that only matter for parsing and not for semantics.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In computer science, an abstract semantic graph (ASG) or term graph is a form of abstract syntax in which an expression of a formal or programming language is represented by a graph whose vertices are the expression's subterms. An ASG is at a higher level of abstraction than an abstract syntax tree (or AST), which is used to express the syntactic structure of an expression or program.

ASGs are more complex and concise than ASTs because they may contain shared subterms (also known as "common subexpressions").[1] Abstract semantic graphs are often used by compilers as an intermediate representation to store the results of performing common subexpression elimination on abstract syntax trees, since ASTs are trees and so cannot represent shared terms. ASGs are usually directed acyclic graphs (DAG), although some applications may permit graphs containing cycles. For example, a graph with a cycle might be used to represent the recursive expressions commonly used in functional programming languages as non-looping iteration constructs. The mutability of these types of graphs is studied in the field of graph rewriting.

The term graph nomenclature is associated with the field of term graph rewriting,[2] which involves transforming and processing expressions by specifying rewriting rules,[3] whereas abstract semantic graph is used when discussing linguistics, programming languages, type systems and compilation.

Abstract syntax trees cannot share subexpression nodes, because a node in a proper tree cannot have more than one parent. This conceptual simplicity is appealing, but it may come at the cost of redundant representation and, in turn, possibly inefficient duplicated computation of identical terms. For this reason ASGs are often used as an intermediate language at a compilation stage subsequent to abstract syntax tree construction via parsing.

An abstract semantic graph is typically constructed from an abstract syntax tree through enrichment and abstraction. The enrichment can for example be the addition of back-pointers: edges from an identifier node (where a variable is used) to a node representing the declaration of that variable. The abstraction can involve removing details that are relevant only in parsing, not for semantics.

References:
[1] Garner, Richard. (2011). An abstract view on syntax with sharing. Journal of Logic and Computation. doi:10.1093/logcom/exr021
[2] Plump, D.. (1999). Handbook of Graph Grammars and Computing by Graph Transformation: applications, languages and tools. World Scientific.
[3] Barendregt, H. P.. (1987). Term graph rewriting. Springer. doi:10.1007/3-540-17945-3_8
